title: Restaurant Table Bookings
prompt: A booking app lets diners reserve restaurant tables for a time slot. During a promotion, many diners try to book the same popular tables at once. Design the tables, indexes and booking step.
facts: 2,000 restaurants, about 20 tables each, 10 time slots a day
Bookings are kept for one year
Peak: about 500 booking attempts per second, many for the same tables
Diners often open "my bookings", which lists their upcoming bookings
A table must never be booked twice for the same slot
scope: Booking a table and listing a diner's bookings
Payment and cancellations are out of scope

requirements: States the rule that one table has at most one booking per slot, and that it must hold even when two diners book at once
Names the two main operations: book a table, list my bookings
estimation: Rows per year: 2,000 × 20 × 10 × 365 = 146 million possible bookings, so lookups need indexes
Or: 500 attempts per second is a write load to confirm with a load test on the real database
design: A bookings table with one row per booking, written by the booking step
data: A unique constraint on (table_id, slot) so the database rejects a second booking for the same table and slot, or a conditional update on a slot row
An index on (diner_id, slot) for "my bookings"
tradeoffs: Explains the race: checking that a table is free, then inserting in a separate step, lets two diners both succeed
Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: each index slows every insert; or a second booking attempt gets an error that the app must turn into "table taken"

fullMarkDesigns: Table bookings(table_id, slot, diner_id) with a unique constraint on (table_id, slot): a booking is a plain insert, and the database rejects a duplicate. An index on (diner_id, slot) serves "my bookings". 146 million rows a year makes the indexes necessary. Trade-off: two indexes add work to each insert; the rejected insert becomes a "table taken" message.

A slots table with one row per table and slot, created ahead of time, booked with UPDATE ... SET diner_id = ? WHERE table_id = ? AND slot = ? AND diner_id IS NULL; 1 row updated means booked, 0 means taken. An index on (diner_id, slot) serves "my bookings". Trade-off: rows must be created in advance for every slot.

assumptions: Slots are fixed times, so a booking is one table and one slot
One database server handles 500 writes per second, confirmed by a load test
reference.design:
Table bookings(table_id, slot, diner_id, created_at). A unique constraint on (table_id, slot) means the database itself refuses a second booking for the same table and slot, so there is no gap between checking and writing: the insert either succeeds or fails.
An index on (diner_id, slot) lets "my bookings" read only that diner's upcoming rows, instead of scanning up to 146 million rows a year (2,000 × 20 × 10 × 365).
Each booking writes the row plus two index entries (the unique constraint's index and the diner index).
alternatives: Check in the application, then insert: simple, but two diners can both pass the check
Lock the table row first: works, but diners wait on each other during the promotion

title: Sign-up and Login for 5 Million Users
prompt: A learning app has 5 million user accounts. Users log in with their email, and the login is getting slow. Sign-ups sometimes create two accounts with the same email. Design the user data.
facts: 5 million users; each account has an id, email, password hash and display name, plus optional profile fields that differ between users
Peak: about 2,000 logins per second and 50 sign-ups per second
A login looks up one user by email
Email must be unique, even when two sign-ups with the same email arrive at the same moment
Measured on this database: a lookup through an index takes about 1 ms; a full scan of the users table takes about 300 ms
scope: Password checking and sessions are out of scope

requirements: States the uniqueness rule for email and that it must hold for simultaneous sign-ups
States a login time target, such as tens of milliseconds
estimation: Without an index, 2,000 logins per second × 300 ms = 600 seconds of scanning work every second, far beyond one database
With an index, 2,000 × 1 ms = 2 seconds of lookup work per second, spread over the database's connections
design: Accounts in a relational table with a primary key on id
data: A unique constraint on email, which also creates the index the login needs
Optional profile fields kept as nullable columns, a JSON column, or a separate profile store, with a reason
tradeoffs: Explains why checking "is this email free?" in application code fails when two sign-ups arrive together
Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: the email index adds work to each of the 50 sign-ups per second, which is small

fullMarkDesigns: Users table with id as primary key and a unique constraint on email. Login looks up by email through the unique index (about 1 ms); a duplicate sign-up fails the constraint and gets "email already used". Optional fields go in a JSON column because they vary. 2,000 × 300 ms of scanning would be impossible; 2,000 × 1 ms is fine.

Accounts in a relational table with a unique email constraint for login and uniqueness, and the varied profile fields in a document store keyed by user id. Login never touches the profile store. Trade-off: two stores to run, in exchange for flexible profiles.

assumptions: Emails are stored in one consistent form, such as lower case
Each login reads one account row
reference.design:
Table users(id primary key, email, password_hash, display_name, profile). A unique constraint on email gives the login its index and makes the database reject a second account with the same email, even when two sign-ups arrive together.
Load: without the index, each of 2,000 logins per second would scan the table for about 300 ms, 600 seconds of work every second; with it, each lookup takes about 1 ms.
Optional profile fields that differ between users go in a JSON column, so adding a field needs no schema change.
alternatives: Check for an existing email in code before inserting: two sign-ups can both pass
Put everything in a document store: flexible, but the unique-email rule must still be enforced by a unique index there
